title: Crestwell Coffee Ltd
context: Crestwell Coffee Ltd runs 46 coffee shops in towns across the Midlands and the North of England. It competes with national chains and independent cafés by focusing on high-quality, ethically sourced coffee. Its target market is professionals aged 25-45 who buy coffee on the way to work.

The business has opened four new shops in the last year, but the price of coffee beans has risen by 38% over two years and the National Living Wage rose by almost 10% in April 2024. Crestwell increased the price of a standard latte from £3.20 to £3.40, but directors fear that further price rises would drive customers to cheaper rivals.

Crestwell's marketing director wants to launch a monthly subscription: for £25 a month, subscribers could collect one hot drink per day. She believes it would 'lock in' loyal customers and attract new ones before a national rival launches a similar scheme. The finance director is less convinced.

title: Northgate Logistics plc
context: Northgate Logistics plc stores and delivers goods for online retailers from five large warehouses in England. Warehouse staff pick and pack orders by hand. Pay is close to the National Living Wage and most staff are on flexible contracts.

Demand for Northgate's services has grown, but its retail customers have complained about late deliveries and picking errors. Two retailers moved their contracts to a rival last year, which uses robots to pick orders.

Northgate's board is considering investing £36m in automated picking systems. The operations director says that this would allow 600 fewer warehouse staff to be employed. The HR director has warned that staff morale is already low.

title: Verde Energy plc
context: Verde Energy plc designs and installs solar panels and home battery systems for UK households. Demand has grown rapidly because of high energy prices and government support for renewable energy, which is due to end in 2026.
At present Verde imports its batteries from China. Battery prices have fallen by around 15% a year, but delivery delays caused problems for installers last winter.

The directors are considering building a battery factory in the UK at a cost of £12m. Production would start in Year 1. The project would be financed entirely by a long-term bank loan at 7% interest a year. The directors have set an investment criterion that projects must have a positive NPV using a discount rate of 8% and pay back within 3 years.

title: PureBloom Cosmetics plc
context: PureBloom Cosmetics plc makes vegan, cruelty-free skincare products sold through UK supermarkets, its own website and 30 PureBloom stores. Its mission is 'beauty that does no harm'. Its products are priced about 20% above mass-market brands.

In January 2024 an environmental campaign group, ClearSeas, criticised PureBloom for packaging most products in single-use plastic. ClearSeas posted its findings on social media and they were widely shared. PureBloom's share price fell from 412p to 371p in the following week.

PureBloom's directors are considering switching to refillable aluminium packaging. This would add an estimated 18p to the cost of each product and would require a £4m investment in new filling equipment.

title: Halden Furniture Ltd
context: Halden Furniture Ltd makes high-quality sofas to order in its factory in Lancashire. Customers choose the size, fabric and colour, and pay a 30% deposit when ordering. The remaining 70% is paid on delivery.

Orders have grown strongly, but the factory is running at 96% capacity utilisation and the average time between order and delivery has risen from 7 to 10 weeks. Rivals deliver in about 6 weeks. Halden holds large inventories of fabric 'just in case' customers choose them.

To reduce lead times, the directors are considering two options. Option 1: outsource the making of wooden sofa frames to a specialist supplier in Poland, freeing factory space for upholstery. Option 2: invest £1.2m in computer-controlled cutting machines, which would increase capacity by 25%.

title: Brightpath Gyms Ltd
context: Brightpath Gyms Ltd operates 60 low-cost gyms across the UK. Each gym has a manager and around eight fitness staff. Until now, all decisions about opening hours, classes and local promotions have been made at head office.

Member retention varies widely between regions. Head office believes this is linked to how engaged staff are. The new chief executive plans to decentralise decision making so that gym managers can tailor classes and promotions to local members.
She also plans to introduce commission for fitness staff: £15 for every new annual membership they sell, alongside their existing hourly pay.

title: Tidewater Foods plc
context: Tidewater Foods plc makes premium sauces and condiments in Devon. 45% of its revenue comes from exports, mainly to the USA and the EU. It imports some ingredients, such as spices and olive oil, which are priced in US dollars and euros.
In 2024 the value of the pound rose against both the dollar and the euro. Tidewater's export director is concerned that US retailers will turn to cheaper American brands.
Tidewater currently sells to the USA by exporting through an agent. It is considering a joint venture with a US food distributor, which would bottle Tidewater's sauces in the USA under licence.

title: Kettle & Co Bakeries Ltd
context: Kettle & Co Bakeries Ltd is a family business with 14 bakery shops in Yorkshire. Each shop bakes its own bread on site. For 60 years the business has been run by members of the Kettle family, who make most decisions personally.

In 2024 the family appointed its first chief executive from outside the family. She plans to close the on-site bakeries and build a central bakery that would supply all shops each morning. She also wants to introduce standard recipes, written procedures and clear job descriptions.
Many long-serving bakers are unhappy. Two family directors oppose the plan, arguing that 'baked in store' is what makes Kettle & Co special.
